### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage

# A v0-style image block that also carries a block id
message = HumanMessage(
    content=[
        {
            "type": "image",
            "source_type": "url",
            "url": "https://example.com/x.png",
            "id": "block-1",
        }
    ]
)

message.content_blocks
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 16, in <module>
    message.content_blocks
  File ".../langchain_core/messages/block_translators/langchain_v0.py", line 83, in ...
    return types.create_image_block(
TypeError: langchain_core.messages.content.create_image_block() got multiple values
for keyword argument 'id'
```

### Description

Converting a legacy v0 content block that carries an `id` raises `TypeError` instead of producing a
v1 block. `content_blocks` is a public property, so this is reachable without touching private API.

Measured on `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`) — every `url`/`base64` source across the three block
types fails, while the `source_type="id"` variants are fine:

| block type / source_type | without `id` | with `id` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `image` / `url` | works | **`TypeError`** |
| `image` / `base64` | works | **`TypeError`** |
| `image` / `id` | works | n/a (`id` is the source) |
| `audio` / `url` | works | **`TypeError`** |
| `audio` / `base64` | works | **`TypeError`** |
| `audio` / `id` | works | n/a |
| `file` / `url` | works | **`TypeError`** |
| `file` / `base64` | works | **`TypeError`** |
| `file` / `id` | works | n/a |

## Root cause

`_extract_v0_extras` collects every key not listed in the branch's `known_keys` and the result is
splatted into the factory call:
```python
known_keys = {"mime_type", "type", "source_type", "url"}
extras = _extract_v0_extras(block, known_keys)
if "id" in block:
    return types.create_image_block(
        url=block["url"],
        mime_type=block.get("mime_type"),
        id=block["id"],      # explicit
        **extras,            # also contains "id"
    )
```

The `url` and `base64` branches omit `"id"` from `known_keys`, so it stays in `extras` and collides
with the explicit `id=` argument. The three `source_type="id"` branches declare
`known_keys = {"type", "source_type", "id"}`, which is why only they work today. Grepping the file:
7 of the 10 `known_keys` sets omit `"id"`, and every one of those branches also passes `id=` and
`**extras` together.

## Proposed fix

Exclude `id` in the helper rather than adding it to seven separate `known_keys` sets:
```python
return {
    k: v for k, v in block_dict.items() if k not in known_keys and k != "id"
}
```

`id` is never an extra — it is either passed explicitly to the factory, or (for
`source_type="id"`) the file reference itself, which those branches already list in `known_keys`.
Doing it once in the helper keeps all ten call sites consistent.

After the change, all six failing combinations convert, and the semantics are preserved:
```text
image/url    + id=block-1   ->  id='block-1'   file_id=None      extras=None
image/base64 + id=block-2   ->  id='block-2'   file_id=None      extras=None
image/id     (file source)  ->  id=None        file_id='file-9'  extras=None
```

Genuine extras still survive:
```text
{"type": "image", "source_type": "url", "url": ..., "id": "block-1",
 "alt_text": "kept", "another": 42}
    -> id='block-1', extras={'alt_text': 'kept', 'another': 42}
```

## Alternatives considered and why they were rejected

- **Add `"id"` to the seven `known_keys` sets.** Same effect but seven edits instead of one, and the
  next branch added would need to remember it again.
- **Pop `id` from `extras` at each call site.** Also repeated seven times, and leaves the helper
  returning a dict that is never safe to splat.
- **Drop the explicit `id=` argument and rely on `**extras`.** Changes behaviour for
  `source_type="id"` blocks, where `id` means the file reference rather than the block id — those
  correctly map to `file_id` today.

## Backwards compatibility

Only affects calls that raise `TypeError` today. `extras` no longer contains `id`, but the block's
`id` field carries it, and `id` was never usable from `extras` because the call raised before
returning. Blocks without an `id` are unchanged, and `source_type="id"` blocks still map to
`file_id`. Verified all four previously-working paths behave identically.

## Verification

Against `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`):

- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy`, `scripts/lint_imports.sh` — all clean
- `langchain-core` unit suite: **2258 passed** (baseline on `master` is 2247). The one failure I see,
  `test_ssrf_protection.py::test_discord_webhook`, is a DNS artifact of my own network and reproduces
  on unmodified `master`.
- Downstream `langchain` (v1) unit suite: **1098 passed**, unchanged
- Reverting the one-line change fails exactly the seven new tests and nothing else

Fix and tests are ready on `gaoanze888/core/v0-block-id-extras`.

except ModelError:
    print("caught as ModelError")
except httpx.TimeoutException as e:
    print(f"escaped as plain httpx: {type(e).__name__}")
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
escaped as plain httpx: ConnectTimeout


No traceback — the problem is that the exception is not classified, so
`except ModelTimeoutError` (or `except ModelError`) never matches.
```

### Description

`ModelError` documents the contract for the standard model exception types added in #39538:

> Subclasses correspond to conditions that model providers report consistently, keyed to the HTTP
> status they surface it with, **so the same condition maps to the same exception type regardless of
> provider**.

For timeouts and connection failures, `langchain-mistralai` does not hold up its side of that.

Coverage of the core types per integration, on `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`), from the classes each
package defines:

| core type | openai | anthropic | fireworks | mistralai |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ModelAuthenticationError` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `ModelPermissionDeniedError` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `ModelInvalidRequestError` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `ModelNotFoundError` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `ModelRateLimitError` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `ModelAPIError` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `ModelTimeoutError` | yes | yes | yes | **no** |
| `ModelConnectionError` | yes | yes | yes | **no** |

## Root cause

`langchain_mistralai` classifies errors only in `_raise_on_error`, which runs on an HTTP *response*:
```python
def _raise_on_error(response: httpx.Response) -> None:
    if httpx.codes.is_error(response.status_code):
        ...
        raise _status_error_type(response.status_code)(...)
```

Timeouts and connection failures never produce a response, so they are raised by `httpx` before that
function is reached and propagate unchanged. The other three integrations convert them explicitly:

- `langchain_openai/chat_models/base.py:671-674` — `isinstance(e, openai.APITimeoutError)` /
  `openai.APIConnectionError`
- `langchain_anthropic/chat_models.py:1019-1021` — same for `anthropic.APITimeoutError` /
  `APIConnectionError`
- `langchain_fireworks/chat_models.py:643-645` — same shape

Measured with a client that raises at the transport layer:

| raised by `httpx` | `mistralai` on `master` | caught by `ModelError`? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `httpx.ConnectTimeout` | `ConnectTimeout` | no |
| `httpx.ReadTimeout` | `ReadTimeout` | no |
| `httpx.ConnectError` | `ConnectError` | no |

The practical consequence is that `is_retryable` is unavailable for these, so the retry middleware
added in #39538 cannot classify a Mistral timeout the way it classifies one from the other three
providers.

## Proposed fix

Add the two missing classes, following exactly the existing pattern in that file (dual inheritance
from the transport exception and the core type):
```python
class MistralAITimeoutError(httpx.TimeoutException, ModelTimeoutError):
    """Mistral AI timeout classified as a LangChain model error."""


class MistralAIConnectionError(httpx.ConnectError, ModelConnectionError):
    """Mistral AI connection failure classified as a LangChain model error."""
```

and convert at the two places the request is issued (`_completion_with_retry` and its async
counterpart), mirroring how the other integrations do it. `ConnectTimeout` subclasses both
`TimeoutException` and `ConnectError`, so the timeout branch has to be checked first.

Result:

| raised by `httpx` | after | `is_retryable` | still catchable as `httpx` type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `httpx.ConnectTimeout` | `MistralAITimeoutError` | `True` | yes |
| `httpx.ReadTimeout` | `MistralAITimeoutError` | `True` | yes |
| `httpx.ConnectError` | `MistralAIConnectionError` | `True` | yes |

## Alternatives considered and why they were rejected

- **Widen `_raise_on_error` to take the exception instead of the response.** It is called from four
  places that all already hold a response; changing its signature touches more code than adding a
  sibling helper for the transport case.
- **Register the transport errors in `_STATUS_ERROR_TYPES`.** That dict is keyed by HTTP status, and
  these failures have no status.
- **Rely on the existing tenacity retry decorator** (`errors = [httpx.RequestError, httpx.StreamError]`).
  That handles retrying inside the integration, but the exception that eventually escapes is still
  unclassified, so callers and the core retry middleware cannot act on it.

## Backwards compatibility

The new classes inherit from the same `httpx` exceptions that were raised before, so existing
`except httpx.TimeoutException` / `except httpx.ConnectError` handlers keep working — verified. Any
transport error outside the two categories keeps its original type.

## Verification

Against `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`):

- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` — clean; `mypy` on `chat_models.py` — 0 errors
  (`embeddings.py:167` reports one, but it does so on unmodified `master` too and is unrelated)
- `langchain-mistralai` unit suite: **101 passed**, 1 skipped (baseline on `master` is 99; the +2 are
  the added test groups)
- Reverting only the wiring at the request site — leaving the helper and its unit tests intact —
  fails exactly the two end-to-end tests. That asymmetry is deliberate: a test that only exercises
  the helper would still pass with the wiring removed, so there is one test per layer.

To be explicit: I found this by auditing the #39538 contract across integrations, not by hitting it
in an application. The argument is the documented cross-provider promise plus the three-out-of-four
asymmetry. Fix and tests are ready on `gaoanze888/mistralai/timeout-connection-errors`.

`langchain-mistralai` and `langchain-core` at `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`), Python 3.12, macOS.

- [ ] langchain-xai
- [ ] Other / not sure / general

### Related Issues / PRs

_No response_

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda, RunnableParallel, RunnablePassthrough

parallel = RunnableParallel(a=RunnablePassthrough(), b=RunnableLambda(lambda x: x))
schema = parallel.get_input_schema()

print(schema.model_json_schema())
# {'properties': {'root': {'title': 'Root'}}, 'required': ['root'], ...}

value = {"k": 1}
print(parallel.invoke(value))   # works: {'a': {'k': 1}, 'b': {'k': 1}}
schema.model_validate(value)    # raises
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
{'a': {'k': 1}, 'b': {'k': 1}}
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 11, in <module>
    schema.model_validate(value)
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for RunnableParallel<a,b>Input
root
  Field required [type=missing, input_value={'k': 1}, input_type=dict]
```

### Description

`get_input_schema()` documents itself as returning "a pydantic model that can be used to validate
input to the `Runnable`". For `RunnableParallel`, no input satisfies both the schema and `invoke`.

Measured on `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`), `RunnableParallel(a=RunnablePassthrough(), b=RunnableLambda(lambda x: x))`:

| input | `invoke` | `get_input_schema().model_validate` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{"k": 1}` | works | **rejected** |
| `"x"` | works | **rejected** |
| `5` | works | **rejected** |
| `[1]` | works | **rejected** |

The only value the schema accepts is `{"root": ...}`, which `invoke` then treats as an ordinary
dict rather than unwrapping it, so it does not express what the schema implies either.

## Root cause

`RunnableParallel.get_input_schema` merges the fields of each step's input schema
(`langchain_core/runnables/base.py:4045-4054`):
```python
return create_model_v2(
    self.get_name("Input"),
    field_definitions={
        k: _get_schema_field_definition(v)
        for step in self.steps__.values()
        for k, v in get_fields(step.get_input_schema(config)).items()
        if k != "__root__"
    },
)
```

A step that accepts any single value reports its input schema as a Pydantic root model. The
synthetic field name for that is `__root__` in Pydantic v1 and **`root`** in v2:
```python
>>> class M(RootModel[int]): pass
>>> list(M.model_fields)
['root']
```

Only the v1 spelling is excluded, so the v2 `root` gets merged in as if it were a caller-supplied
key. This looks like a leftover from the v1 → v2 migration.

Steps whose schemas expose `root` include `RunnablePassthrough` and any `RunnableLambda` without an
annotated parameter — both are ordinary building blocks, and mixing one of them with a step that has
real fields pollutes the merged schema too:

| parallel steps | resulting schema |
| --- | --- |
| `Passthrough` + unannotated `Lambda` | `required=['root']` |
| `Passthrough` + `PromptTemplate("{a}")` | `required=['root', 'a']` |
| two `PromptTemplate`s | `required=['a', 'b']` — already correct |

## Proposed fix

Exclude both spellings:
```python
if k not in {"__root__", "root"}
```

Result on the same three combinations:

| parallel steps | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Passthrough` + `Lambda` | `required=['root']`, dict rejected | `properties={}`, dict accepted |
| `Passthrough` + `PromptTemplate` | `required=['root', 'a']`, dict rejected | `properties=['a']`, dict accepted |
| two `PromptTemplate`s | correct | unchanged |

## Alternatives considered and why they were rejected

- **Return the root-model schema itself when every step exposes `root`.** The existing code already
  does something like this earlier in the method, but only when the root field's annotation is not
  `Any`. For `RunnablePassthrough`/`RunnableLambda` the annotation *is* `Any`, so that branch is
  deliberately skipped — reusing it here would change which schema is returned for the mixed case
  (`Passthrough` + `PromptTemplate`), where the real fields must survive.
- **Make `invoke` accept `{"root": ...}` by unwrapping it.** That changes runtime behaviour to match
  a schema that is itself wrong, and would break callers who legitimately pass a dict with a `root`
  key.
- **Match on the field name only when the annotation is `Any`.** Narrower, but `root`/`__root__` are
  reserved synthetic names in either case; a step that genuinely wants a caller-supplied key called
  `root` cannot express it through a root model anyway.

## Backwards compatibility

The merged schema loses a field that no caller could satisfy, and gains nothing. Combinations whose
schemas were already correct (no step exposing `root`) are unchanged — verified on the two
`PromptTemplate` case above. Pydantic v1 paths are untouched: the two early-return branches for
`__root__` still run first, and the existing v1 tests
(`test_runnable_parallel_uses_base_schema_for_v1_root_model`,
`test_runnable_sequence_v1_input_schema`, `test_runnable_branch_v1_input_schema`) all still pass.

## Verification

Against `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`):

- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy`, `scripts/lint_imports.sh` — all clean
- `langchain-core` unit suite: **2253 passed** (baseline on `master` is 2247; the added tests plus
  the v1 root-model tests account for the difference). The one failure I see,
  `test_ssrf_protection.py::test_discord_webhook`, is a DNS artifact of my own network and
  reproduces on unmodified `master`.
- Downstream `langchain` (v1) unit suite: **1098 passed**, unchanged from `master`.
- Reverting the one-line change while keeping the tests fails exactly the two new tests and nothing
  else; the pre-existing Pydantic v1 tests keep passing.

To be explicit about what this report is: I found it by auditing `get_input_schema()` against the
inputs `invoke()` accepts, not by hitting it in an application. I am not claiming production impact —
the argument is the self-contradiction plus the asymmetry with combinations that already work. If
that is not worth a change on its own, please close this.

Fix and two regression tests are ready on `gaoanze888/core/parallel-input-schema-root`.

### System Info

`langchain-core` at `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`, includes `release(core): 1.6.0`), Python 3.12,
macOS.

the commit named._

from langchain_core.load import dumps, loads
from langchain_core.prompts.image import ImagePromptTemplate

# ImagePromptValue is what the public ImagePromptTemplate.format_prompt() returns
template = ImagePromptTemplate(
    template={"url": "https://example.com/{name}.png"},
    input_variables=["name"],

prompt_value = template.format_prompt(name="cat")
print(type(prompt_value).__name__)   # ImagePromptValue

loads(serialized)                    # raises
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
ImagePromptValue
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 13, in <module>
    loads(serialized)
ValueError: Deserialization of ('langchain', 'schema', 'prompt', 'ImagePromptValue') is not
allowed. The default (allowed_objects='core') only permits core langchain-core classes.
```

### Description

`ImagePromptValue` declares itself serializable and `dumps()` produces valid output, but it is
absent from the deserialization allowlist in `langchain_core/load/mapping.py`, so `loads()`
rejects the very id that `dumps()` wrote. Its three siblings in the same module all round-trip.

Measured on `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`), `loads(dumps(obj))` for every class in
`langchain_core.prompt_values`:

| class | round-trip |
| --- | --- |
| `StringPromptValue` | works |
| `ChatPromptValue` | works |
| `ChatPromptValueConcrete` | works |
| `ImagePromptValue` | **`ValueError`** |

Three of four are mapped, so the omission reads as an oversight rather than a deliberate
exclusion. `is_lc_serializable()` returning `True` is the class's own promise that a round trip
works, so the current state is the code contradicting itself.

`ImagePromptValue` is what the public `ImagePromptTemplate.format_prompt()` returns, so it is
reachable without touching private API:
```text
ImagePromptTemplate.format_prompt(name="cat")  ->  ImagePromptValue
dumps(prompt_value)                            ->  186 chars, no error
loads(serialized)                              ->  ValueError
```

To be explicit about what this report is and is not: I found this by scanning all 68 classes in
`langchain-core` that report `is_lc_serializable() == True` and attempting a round trip on each,
not by hitting it in an application. I am not claiming user reports or production impact - the
argument is only the self-contradiction and the asymmetry with the three siblings. If that is not
worth a change on its own, please close this.

## Root cause

`langchain_core/load/mapping.py` holds two allowlists - one keyed by the legacy `langchain`
namespace and one by the current `langchain_core` namespace. `StringPromptValue`,
`ChatPromptValue` and `ChatPromptValueConcrete` each appear in both. `ImagePromptValue` appears
in neither.

## Proposed fix

Add the two missing entries, mirroring how the siblings are registered:
```python
# legacy namespace block
("langchain", "schema", "prompt", "ImagePromptValue"): (
    "langchain_core",
    "prompt_values",
    "ImagePromptValue",
),

# langchain_core namespace block
("langchain_core", "prompt_values", "ImagePromptValue"): (
    "langchain_core",
    "prompt_values",
    "ImagePromptValue",
),
```

The legacy key is `("langchain", "schema", "prompt", ...)` because that is what
`ImagePromptValue.get_lc_namespace()` returns - I read the id emitted by `dumps()` rather than
assuming it follows the `("langchain", "prompts", ...)` shape its siblings use.

## Alternatives considered and why they were rejected

- **Make `is_lc_serializable()` return `False`.** Removes a declared capability and would break
  anyone currently calling `dumps()` successfully; also diverges from the three siblings.
- **Tell users to pass `allowed_objects="all"`.** Widens the allowlist far beyond one class and
  defeats the `"core"` default, whose purpose is that core classes work without it.
- **Register only in the `langchain_core` block.** `dumps()` emits the legacy id, so that alone
  would not fix the failure.

## Backwards compatibility

Additive only - two allowlist entries. Nothing that deserialized before changes behaviour, and no
public API is touched.

## Verification

Against `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`):

- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy`, `scripts/lint_imports.sh` - all clean
- `langchain-core` unit suite: **2249 passed** (baseline on `master` is 2247). The one failure I
  see, `test_ssrf_protection.py::test_discord_webhook`, is a DNS artifact of my own network and
  reproduces on unmodified `master`.
- Downstream `langchain` (v1) unit suite: **1098 passed**, unchanged from `master`.
- Reverting the two entries while keeping the test fails exactly the new test and nothing else;
  the neighbouring `test_runnable_pick_roundtrips` keeps passing.

Same defect family as #39752, fixed in #39753 (`ded2a1fb3`) for `RunnablePick`. Fix and
regression test are ready on `gaoanze888/core/serializable-image-prompt-value`.

body:

- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.

### Package (Required)

- [ ] langchain
- [ ] langchain-openai
- [ ] langchain-anthropic
- [ ] langchain-classic
- [x] langchain-core
- [ ] langchain-model-profiles

- [ ] langchain-huggingface

- [ ] langchain-nomic
- [ ] langchain-ollama
- [ ] langchain-openrouter
- [ ] langchain-perplexity
- [ ] langchain-qdrant
- [ ] langchain-xai
- [ ] Other / not sure / general

### Related Issues / PRs

_No response_

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda


class FalseyError(RuntimeError):
    """An exception whose truth value is False."""

    def __bool__(self) -> bool:
        return False


attempts = 0


def always_fail(_x: int) -> int:
    global attempts
    attempts += 1
    raise FalseyError("boom")


runnable = RunnableLambda(always_fail).with_retry(
    stop_after_attempt=3, wait_exponential_jitter=False
)
runnable.batch([0], return_exceptions=True)

print(f"attempts={attempts}")   # expected 3, actual 1
assert attempts == 3
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
attempts=1
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 29, in <module>
    assert attempts == 3
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AssertionError

No exception is raised from batch() itself - the failure is silent. with_retry(...) is
configured for 3 attempts but the underlying callable is invoked only once.
```

### Description

`RunnableRetry._batch` decides whether an attempt failed by testing the collected exception for
**truthiness** instead of comparing against `None`. An exception that overrides `__bool__` (or
`__len__`) to be falsey therefore never gets re-raised to `tenacity`, the attempt is recorded as a
success, and no retry happens.

`langchain_core/runnables/retry.py:262-272` (`_batch`):
```python
first_exception = None
for offset, r in enumerate(result):
    if isinstance(r, Exception):
        if not first_exception:        # <- truthiness, not `is None`
            first_exception = r
        continue
    orig_idx = remaining_indices[offset]
    results_map[orig_idx] = r
# If any exception occurred, raise it, to retry the failed ones
if first_exception:                    # <- truthiness again
    raise first_exception
```

With a falsey exception, `first_exception` stays falsey, so `raise first_exception` never executes.
`tenacity` sees the attempt return normally, `attempt.retry_state.outcome.failed` is `False`, and
the loop stops after one pass.

`_abatch` (lines 337-347) contains the identical three lines and behaves identically.

Measured against `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`), `stop_after_attempt=3`, one input:

| exception raised by the callable | invocations of the underlying callable |
| --- | --- |
| `RuntimeError` (ordinary) | 3 |
| `FalseyError` (`__bool__` returns `False`) | **1** |

`abatch` shows the same 3 vs 1 split.

**Why this is not a contrived case.** Any exception class that also implements a container-ish or
"empty" protocol inherits Python's `__len__`-based truthiness. A concrete example is an exception
that subclasses both `Exception` and a collection type to carry a list of validation failures:
when that list is empty, the exception is falsey. Users hitting this see retries silently not
happening, with no error to trace back to `langchain-core`. The same anti-pattern has already been
recognised as a bug elsewhere in core - #39699 (`fix(core): finalize chain-group runs on
BaseException`) and the open #38469 are the same family of "exception object treated as a boolean
or narrowed type" defects.

**Scope.** This is only about the truthiness test. `_invoke`/`_ainvoke` do not go through this code
path and are unaffected. `isinstance(r, Exception)` is left alone deliberately - see below.

## Proposed fix

Compare against `None` explicitly, in both `_batch` and `_abatch`:
```python
first_exception: Exception | None = None
for offset, r in enumerate(result):
    if isinstance(r, Exception):
        # Compare against `None`: an exception overriding `__bool__`/`__len__` is
        # falsey, and a truthiness check would skip the retry entirely.
        if first_exception is None:
            first_exception = r
        continue
    orig_idx = remaining_indices[offset]
    results_map[orig_idx] = r
if first_exception is not None:
    raise first_exception
```

## Alternatives considered and why they were rejected

- **Widen `isinstance(r, Exception)` to `BaseException`.** Tempting, since `_batch` consumes
  `super().batch(..., return_exceptions=True)`. But I verified that plain
  `Runnable.batch(return_exceptions=True)` *propagates* a `BaseException` that is not an
  `Exception` rather than collecting it, so such a value cannot reach this loop. Widening the
  check would be dead code here, and would conflate this fix with #38469, which is about
  `BaseChatModel.agenerate`. Out of scope.
- **Normalise the exception (e.g. wrap it) so it becomes truthy.** That changes what the caller
  receives from `batch(return_exceptions=True)` and what `retry_if_exception_type` matches
  against - a behaviour change to fix a comparison bug.
- **Add guards further down instead.** The two lines above are the only place the value's
  truthiness is consulted; anything larger is unnecessary.

## Backwards compatibility

No public API change. The only behavioural difference is for exceptions that are falsey, which
previously bypassed retrying entirely - code relying on that would have been relying on retries
silently not happening. Ordinary exceptions are unaffected: the "ordinary `RuntimeError`" row
above is 3 invocations both before and after.

## Verification

Against `upstream/master` (`3478c28ef`):

- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy`, `scripts/lint_imports.sh` - all clean
- `langchain-core` unit suite: **2249 passed** (baseline on `master` is 2247; the +2 are the new
  tests). The one failure I see, `test_ssrf_protection.py::test_discord_webhook`, is a DNS
  artifact of my own network and reproduces on unmodified `master`.
- Downstream `langchain` (v1) unit suite: **1098 passed**, unchanged from `master`.
- Reverting the fix while keeping the tests fails exactly the two new tests
  (`test_retry_batch_retries_falsey_exception`,
  `test_async_retry_batch_retries_falsey_exception`) and no others; the four pre-existing retry
  tests keep passing.

I have the fix and both regression tests ready on `gaoanze888/core/retry-falsey-exception` and can
open a PR as soon as this is assigned.

### Related Issues / PRs

Same family as #39678 / #39680 (`dict` → `Mapping` in the mustache lookup) and #39743
(the same distinction at the prompt input boundary), but the primary problem here is a
crash rather than a type-tolerance gap.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
Runs as-is in a fresh interpreter, no API key or network required.


from langchain_core.utils.function_calling import convert_to_openai_function


def my_func(x: int, y: str) -> str:
    """Do something.

    Args:
        x: A number.
        y: A string.
    """
    return y * x


print(convert_to_openai_function(my_func))


Output:


AttributeError: module 'langchain_core' has no attribute 'tools'


Adding a single unrelated import makes it work:


import langchain_core.tools  # noqa: F401  <- only difference

from langchain_core.utils.function_calling import convert_to_openai_function
# ... same code as above now prints the schema
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 14, in <module>
    print(convert_to_openai_function(my_func))
  File ".../langchain_core/utils/function_calling.py", line 450, in convert_to_openai_function
    elif isinstance(function, langchain_core.tools.base.BaseTool):
                              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: module 'langchain_core' has no attribute 'tools'
```

### Description

`convert_to_openai_function` reaches the `BaseTool` class through the parent package:
```python
elif isinstance(function, langchain_core.tools.base.BaseTool):
```

`function_calling` only does `import langchain_core` at module scope, and importing a
package does not bind its submodules. So `langchain_core.tools` is an attribute of
`langchain_core` only once something else has imported it, and in a process that has not,
the check raises `AttributeError` before it can run.

Which inputs are affected follows from the branch order — anything that reaches that
`elif` crashes:

| input | result in a fresh process |
| --- | --- |
| `dict` | ok (returns from an earlier branch) |
| `pydantic.BaseModel` subclass | ok (earlier branch) |
| `TypedDict` | ok (earlier branch) |
| **plain callable** | **`AttributeError`** |
| non-`dict` `Mapping` | `AttributeError` |

Converting a plain function is the primary documented use of this helper, so the crash is
easy to hit: a script that only imports `convert_to_openai_function` to build tool schemas
never imports `langchain_core.tools`.

It has stayed hidden because `convert_to_openai_tool` — the more common entry point —
starts with `from langchain_core.tools import Tool` (commented "Import locally to prevent
circular import"). That import binds the submodule as a side effect, so anything going
through `convert_to_openai_tool` is protected, and only direct calls to
`convert_to_openai_function` crash. Two more lines in the same module rely on the same side
effect: `langchain_core.tools.base.create_schema_from_function` and
`isinstance(tool, langchain_core.tools.simple.Tool)`.

**A second, smaller problem in the same function.** Both `convert_to_openai_function` and
`convert_to_openai_tool` annotate their first argument as `Mapping[str, Any]`:
```python
def convert_to_openai_tool(
    tool: Mapping[str, Any] | type[BaseModel] | Callable[..., Any] | BaseTool, ...
) -> dict[str, Any]:
```

but every format check inside dispatches on `isinstance(function, dict)`. A `ChainMap`,
`UserDict` or `MappingProxyType` misses all of them and ends up in the unsupported-input
branch with `ValueError: Unsupported function`. A type checker accepts the call, so this
only shows up at runtime. Relatedly, the well-known-tool passthrough in
`convert_to_openai_tool` does `return tool`, so a mapping input is returned unchanged even
though the declared return type is `dict[str, Any]`.

Expected behaviour: converting a callable should not depend on unrelated import order, and
a `Mapping` should be accepted where the annotation says `Mapping`.

I have both fixed locally — a local `from langchain_core.tools import BaseTool` for the
crash, and normalising a non-`dict` mapping once at the entry point so the existing format
detection is untouched — with 22 regression tests. Happy to open a PR; let me know if you

### Related Issues / PRs

Not aware of an existing report — searched for `RunnablePick`, `"is not allowed" Deserialization`
and related terms and found nothing covering this.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
Runs as-is, no API key or network required.


from langchain_core.load import dumpd, load
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough

chain = RunnablePassthrough().pick(["a"])

payload = dumpd(chain)   # works
print(load(payload))     # raises


Output:


ValueError: Deserialization of ('langchain', 'schema', 'runnable', 'RunnablePick') is not
allowed. The default allowed objects ...


Its siblings from the same module round-trip fine, which is what makes this look like an
omission rather than a deliberate restriction:


from langchain_core.load import dumpd, load
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough, RunnablePick

load(dumpd(RunnablePassthrough()))   # ok
load(dumpd(RunnablePick(keys="a")))  # ValueError
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
ValueError: Deserialization of ('langchain', 'schema', 'runnable', 'RunnablePick') is not
allowed. The default allowed objects do not include this class.
```

### Description

`RunnablePick` reports `is_lc_serializable() is True` and `dumpd`/`dumps` produce a payload
for it, but `langchain_core/load/mapping.py` has no entry for it, so `load` refuses to
reconstruct it. `grep -c RunnablePick langchain_core/load/mapping.py` returns `0`, while
`RunnablePassthrough` and `RunnableAssign` — declared in the same
`langchain_core/runnables/passthrough.py` — each have two entries (the legacy
`langchain.schema.runnable` path and the current `langchain_core.runnables.passthrough` one).

All three report `is_lc_serializable() is True`:
```text
RunnablePassthrough    is_lc_serializable=True  module=langchain_core.runnables.passthrough
RunnableAssign         is_lc_serializable=True  module=langchain_core.runnables.passthrough
RunnablePick           is_lc_serializable=True  module=langchain_core.runnables.passthrough
```

The practical effect is that any chain built with the public `Runnable.pick()` helper can be
serialized but not deserialized — `dumpd` and `dumps` both succeed, and the failure only
appears when something tries to read the payload back, which is typically a different process
or a later run than the one that wrote it.

I found this while round-tripping every class in `langchain_core` that reports
`is_lc_serializable()`; of the 32 I could construct, `RunnablePick` was the only one that
dumped successfully but failed to load.

Expected behaviour: a class that declares itself serializable and dumps without error should
be loadable, matching its siblings. Adding the two mapping entries is enough.

I have that change plus two regression tests locally (`RunnablePick` directly, and a chain
built via `.pick()`); both fail without it. Happy to open a PR.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
# ---- Bug 1: Language.PERL not implemented ----
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter, Language

try:
    # PERL exists in enum but is not implemented in separator logic
    RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.from_language(
        Language.PERL,
        chunk_size=10,
        chunk_overlap=0
    )
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Bug 1 Error: {e}")


# ---- Bug 2: InMemoryCache eviction bug ----
from langchain_core.caches import InMemoryCache

cache = InMemoryCache(maxsize=2)

cache.update("prompt_1", "llm_1", "val1")
cache.update("prompt_2", "llm_2", "val2")

# Cache is now at maxsize.
# Updating an existing key SHOULD NOT evict another entry.
cache.update("prompt_2", "llm_2", "val2_new_value")

# Expected: prompt_1 still exists
print("Cache keys:", list(cache._cache.keys()))
print("Bug 2: Is prompt_1 still in cache?",
      ("prompt_1", "llm_1") in cache._cache)
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
# Bug 1
ValueError: Language Language.PERL is not implemented yet!

# Bug 2 (Observed Behavior)
Bug 2: Is prompt_1 still in cache? False
```

### Description

There are two distinct bugs grouped here:

1) Language.PERL is correctly defined in the Language enum, but the switch statement inside get_separators_for_language does not handle it, resulting in a fall-through ValueError instead of appropriately fetching Perl-specific separators.
2) InMemoryCache.update() shrinks the cache incorrectly. When the cache is at its exact maxsize, and you call update() using a key that already exists in the cache, the code checks len(cache) == maxsize and forcefully evicts the oldest entry anyway, lowering the cache size instead of performing an in-place update.


I have already pushed a Branch fixing both issues (adding Perl separators for sub, package, do, eval, etc., and adding an eviction safety guard for InMemoryCache) to my fork and am ready to raise the associated PR closing this issue!

body:

### Package (Required)

- [x] langchain-core

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
from langchain_core.utils.json import parse_partial_json

# Raw carriage return inside a JSON string value
result = parse_partial_json('{"key": "line1\rline2"}')
print(result)  # raises json.JSONDecodeError

# Raw tab inside a JSON string value
result = parse_partial_json('{"key": "col1\tcol2"}')
print(result)  # raises json.JSONDecodeError

# Raw newline works fine because it's already handled
result = parse_partial_json('{"key": "line1\nline2"}')
print(result)  # {'key': 'line1\nline2'} -- OK
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```
json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Invalid control character at: line 1 column 15 (char 14)
```

### Description

`parse_partial_json` already escapes raw `\n` characters inside JSON strings (since they're illegal unescaped per RFC 8259). But it doesn't handle `\r` or `\t`, which are also control characters that must be escaped in JSON strings. Some models emit these raw control characters in their output, causing the parser to fail.

The fix is to add the same escaping pattern for `\r` and `\t` that already exists for `\n`.

body:

### Package

- [x] langchain-core

### Related Issues / PRs

None found.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
from copy import deepcopy

from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage


for content in [
    "hello",
    [{"type": "custom", "payload": "value", "index": 3}],
]:
    message = AIMessage(
        content=content,
        response_metadata={"model_provider": "bedrock_converse"},
    )
    original = deepcopy(message.content)
    first = message.content_blocks
    second = message.content_blocks

    print("original:", original)
    print("content after reads:", message.content)
    print("first read:", first)
    print("second read:", second)
```

Output for the non-standard block:
```text
original: [{"type": "custom", "payload": "value", "index": 3}]
content after reads: [{"type": "custom", "payload": "value"}]
first read: [{"type": "non_standard", "value": {"type": "custom", "payload": "value"}, "index": 3}]
second read: [{"type": "non_standard", "value": {"type": "custom", "payload": "value"}}]
```

String content is similarly replaced with a list after the first read.

### Error Message and Stack Trace

No exception is raised.

### Description

Reading `AIMessage.content_blocks` for a Bedrock Converse message mutates the source message. String content is assigned back as a text-block list, while an unrecognized block with an `index` loses that field because the translator pops it from the original dictionary.

I expect `content_blocks` to derive a standard representation without changing `message.content`, as the property is read-only and other provider translators preserve the source message. Currently two consecutive reads can return different results, and downstream code loses the original Bedrock block index.

If the approach is acceptable, I would like to fix this by using a local list for string conversion and copying an unrecognized block before moving its `index` into the standard wrapper. I can add regression coverage for both `AIMessage` and `AIMessageChunk`. Please assign this issue to me if you approve the proposed solution.

### Related Issues / PRs

- Commit [`27add913`](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/commit/27add913) added `_validate_path()` and threaded  `allow_dangerous_paths` through the loaders, including `_load_examples`. But  `_validate_path` is purely lexical (rejects absolute paths and `..` only), so it does not catch symlinks.
- Commit [`0b5f2c08ee`](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/commit/0b5f2c08ee) recognized that a symlink defeats that lexical check andadded `template_path.resolve()` to `_load_template` (resolving symlinks before the suffix/location is trusted). The equivalent change was never applied to `_load_examples`, which still calls `path.open()` without resolving.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
import json, os, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from langchain_core.prompts.loading import _load_examples

# A file that lives OUTSIDE the current working directory:
outside = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "data.json"
outside.write_text(json.dumps([{"note": "this file is outside the cwd"}]))

# A relative symlink in the cwd (name has no "..", ends in .json) pointing to it:
ws = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()); os.chdir(ws)
os.symlink(outside, "examples.json")           # symlink target is outside the cwd

# allow_dangerous_paths=False is the default; _validate_path only accepts relative,
# non-".." paths, so you would expect the load to stay within the cwd:
print(_load_examples({"examples": "examples.json"}, allow_dangerous_paths=False))
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
No exception, but the result is incorrect. With `allow_dangerous_paths=False`, `_load_examples` returns the contents of a file located outside the working directory when accessed through a relative symlink.
```

### Description

**What I expect.** With `allow_dangerous_paths=False`, a path that *resolves* outside the working directory should be rejected — consistent with `_load_template` (which calls `.resolve()`) and with the file toolkit's `get_validated_relative_path` (which resolves and confines).

**What happens.** `_validate_path()` only performs lexical checks (`path.is_absolute()` and `".." in path.parts`); it never resolves symlinks. `_load_examples()` then calls `path.open()` without resolving, so a relative symlink that contains no `..` and is not absolute passes validation and is followed by the OS at open time. The suffix check (`path.suffix`) also inspects the symlink *name*, not the real target.

**Root cause.** `libs/core/langchain_core/prompts/loading.py`:

- `_validate_path` (lines ~22–46): lexical only, no `resolve()`.
- `_load_examples` (lines ~117–139): `_validate_path(path)` then `path.open()` — no `resolve()`:
  ```python
  path = Path(config["examples"])
  if not allow_dangerous_paths:
      _validate_path(path)          # lexical check passes for a relative symlink
  with path.open(encoding="utf-8") as f:   # OS follows the symlink
      if path.suffix == ".json":    # suffix taken from the symlink name
          examples = json.load(f)
  ```
- `_load_template` (lines ~86–114): already hardened —
  ```python
  _validate_path(template_path)
  resolved_path = template_path.resolve()   # <-- _load_examples has no equivalent
  ```

**Fix.** Resolve then confine in `_load_examples`, mirroring `_load_template` / `get_validated_relative_path`:
```python
resolved = path.resolve()
# reject if `resolved` is absolute / escapes the intended base directory, then:
with resolved.open(encoding="utf-8") as f:
    if resolved.suffix == ".json":
        examples = json.load(f)
    elif resolved.suffix in {".yaml", ".yml"}:
        examples = yaml.safe_load(f)
```

### Related Issues / PRs

- #38005 widened `ToolExceptionHandlerOutput` from `list[...]` to `Sequence[...]` so tuple content
  round-trips.
- #39680 changed `mustache._get_key` to dispatch on `Mapping` instead of the concrete `dict`.

Same widening here, on the config argument.



### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
# No API key or network needed. Only model construction is stubbed, so the
# batch_as_completed path itself runs unmodified.
from unittest.mock import patch

from langchain_core.language_models.fake_chat_models import FakeChatModel

from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

model = init_chat_model()


def run(config):
    with patch(
        "langchain.chat_models.base._init_chat_model_helper", return_value=FakeChatModel()
    ):
        return [
            output
            for _, output in model.batch_as_completed(["hello"], config=config)
        ]


print("list  [{...}] :", run([{"tags": ["test"]}]))
print("tuple ({...},):", run(({"tags": ["test"]},)))

# Observed on master (85602c3676), langchain 1.3.15 / langchain-core 1.6.0:
#
# list  [{...}] : [AIMessage(content='fake response', ...)]
# tuple ({...},): AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'items'
#
# abatch_as_completed fails identically.
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 23, in <module>
    print("tuple ({...},):", run(({"tags": ["test"]},)))
  File "repro.py", line 18, in run
    for _, output in model.batch_as_completed(["hello"], config=config)
  File ".../langchain/chat_models/base.py", line 877, in batch_as_completed
    yield from self._model(cast("RunnableConfig", config)).batch_as_completed(  # type: ignore[call-overload]
  File ".../langchain/chat_models/base.py", line 712, in _model
    params = {**self._default_config, **self._model_params(config)}
  File ".../langchain/chat_models/base.py", line 719, in _model_params
    config = ensure_config(config)
  File ".../langchain_core/runnables/config.py", line 288, in ensure_config
    for k, v in config.items()
AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'items'
```

### Description

**What I expect.** A singleton tuple of configs behaves like a singleton list. Both methods declare
a `Sequence`, matching the base `Runnable` they override:

    # langchain/chat_models/base.py
    # batch_as_completed (~line 864), abatch_as_completed (~line 893)
    config: RunnableConfig | Sequence[RunnableConfig] | None = None

    # langchain_core/runnables/base.py, Runnable.batch_as_completed (~line 1001)
    config: RunnableConfig | Sequence[RunnableConfig] | None = None

**What happens.** The tuple raises `AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'items'` from
inside `langchain_core`, so the traceback points at `ensure_config` rather than at the caller.

**Why this is a bug rather than an unsupported input.**

| Call | Declared type | Singleton tuple |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Runnable.batch_as_completed` (base) | `Sequence[RunnableConfig]` | works |
| `_ConfigurableModel.batch_as_completed` | `Sequence[RunnableConfig]` | crashes |
| `_ConfigurableModel.abatch_as_completed` | `Sequence[RunnableConfig]` | crashes |
| `_ConfigurableModel.batch` / `abatch` | `list[RunnableConfig]` | outside contract |

The override rejects an input its own annotation accepts, and that the base class handles.

**Root cause.** The single-config branch unwraps only a concrete `list`:

    # langchain/chat_models/base.py, ~line 875
    if isinstance(config, list):
        config = config[0]

while the parameter is declared `Sequence[RunnableConfig]`. Any other `Sequence` skips the unwrap and
is passed on as-is, so it reaches `ensure_config`, which requires a mapping. A `cast` on the following
line suppresses the type error that would otherwise flag this.

**Scope.** Two or more configs with a matching number of inputs take the
`super().batch_as_completed()` path and are normalized correctly through `get_config_list`. Only the
singleton non-`list` sequence hits the manual unwrap.

**Precedent inside `langchain_core`.** The helper that exists for exactly this input dispatches on the
abstract ABC rather than the concrete type:

    # langchain_core/runnables/config.py, get_config_list (~line 339)
    if isinstance(config, Sequence):
        return list(map(ensure_config, config))

**Impact.** The affected case is uncommon but valid: callers preserving config collections as
immutable tuples can pass an input accepted by the public annotation and receive an unrelated
`AttributeError` from inside `langchain_core`.

**Expected.** A singleton tuple is unwrapped like a singleton list, so both forms behave identically.

body:

- [ ] langchain-openrouter

- [ ] langchain-xai
- [ ] Other / not sure / general

### Related Issues / PRs

The sibling `ChildTool._injected_args_keys` (langchain_core/tools/base.py) had this exact bug and
was fixed in #39202 (resolving #34558), which added `get_type_hints(include_extras=True)` resolution
instead of raw `signature().parameters` annotations. That fix's own comment explicitly notes:
"StructuredTool overrides this to inspect its wrapped func/coroutine instead" -- but never touched
`StructuredTool._injected_args_keys` in tools/structured.py, which still has the unresolved-annotation
bug the sibling fix just proved unsafe. #34558 (the original report) was exclusively about BaseTool
subclassing and never mentioned StructuredTool.

Not related to #36221 (open, but a mypy "Any" return-type inference complaint about this same method
-- a static-typing issue, not the runtime resolution bug here) or #34770 (open, a Pydantic
model_dump() serialization warning for ToolRuntime -- different root cause).


### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel
from langchain_core.tools import tool, InjectedToolArg

class QueryInput(BaseModel):
    query: str

@tool(args_schema=QueryInput)
def my_tool(query: str, secret: Annotated[str, InjectedToolArg]) -> str:
    """Echo query with secret."""
    return f"{query}-{secret}"

print(my_tool._injected_args_keys)  # frozenset() -- should contain 'secret'
my_tool.invoke({"query": "hi", "secret": "topsecret"})  # raises TypeError

# Control -- remove the top-level `from __future__ import annotations` (only change) and it works:
#   frozenset({'secret'})
#   'hi-topsecret'
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File "...\langchain_core\tools\structured.py", line 97, in _run
    return self.func(*args, **kwargs)
TypeError: my_tool() missing 1 required positional argument: 'secret'
```

### Description

`StructuredTool._injected_args_keys` (tools/structured.py) determines which parameters of the
wrapped function are runtime-injected (`ToolRuntime`, `InjectedToolArg`, `InjectedToolCallId`) by
checking `signature(fn).parameters.items()` and testing the raw `.annotation` on each parameter.
When annotations are postponed -- via `from __future__ import annotations` (PEP 563, a common modern
idiom) or a quoted forward reference -- `.annotation` is a plain unresolved string (e.g.
`"Annotated[str, InjectedToolArg]"`), so the injected-arg check never matches. The injected key is
then missing from `_injected_args_keys`, so it's never re-injected into the call at invoke time,
and the wrapped function raises a plain `TypeError` for a missing positional argument.

This is precisely the bug already fixed for the `ChildTool` (BaseTool-subclassing) fallback in #39202,
which switched to `get_type_hints(fn, include_extras=True)` for resolution. That fix's own comment
acknowledges `StructuredTool` has a separate implementation for this -- it just didn't update it.

Providing a narrower `args_schema` to hide runtime-injected args from the model, combined with
`@tool`/`StructuredTool.from_function` (the primary documented way to create tools), is a documented,
tested pattern. Postponed annotations are common enough (PEP 563-recommended, or just avoiding
circular imports with a quoted forward ref) that this is a plausible, silent, agent-runtime crash
for real tool definitions -- not a typing nit.

Proposed fix: reuse the existing `_get_type_hints(fn, include_extras=True)` helper already defined
in `tools/base.py` (added by #39202 for exactly this purpose) inside
`StructuredTool._injected_args_keys`, mirroring the resolution `ChildTool` now does. Happy to open
a PR with this fix plus regression tests (mirroring the `..._postponed_annotation` test names already
added for `ChildTool` in #39202) if a maintainer can confirm the approach and assign me to this issue.

title: Support custom token_counter in ContextEditingMiddleware (approximate counting under-counts CJK 2-3x)
body:
### Submission checklist

- [x] This is a feature request, not a bug report or usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes the feature request.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar feature request and didn't find it.
- [x] I checked the LangChain documentation and API reference to see if this feature already exists.
- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.

### Package (Required)

- [x] langchain
- [ ] langchain-openai
- [ ] langchain-anthropic
- [ ] langchain-classic
- [ ] langchain-core
- [ ] langchain-model-profiles
- [ ] langchain-tests
- [ ] langchain-text-splitters
- [ ] langchain-chroma
- [ ] langchain-deepseek
- [ ] langchain-exa
- [ ] langchain-fireworks
- [ ] langchain-groq
- [ ] langchain-huggingface
- [ ] langchain-mistralai
- [ ] langchain-nomic
- [ ] langchain-ollama
- [ ] langchain-openrouter
- [ ] langchain-perplexity
- [ ] langchain-qdrant
- [ ] langchain-xai
- [ ] Other / not sure / general

### Feature Description

`ContextEditingMiddleware` currently selects its token counter internally: `token_count_method` accepts only `"approximate"` (which calls `count_tokens_approximately` with default settings) or `"model"` (which requires the chat model to implement `get_num_tokens_from_messages`). There is no way to supply a custom counter.

I would like an optional `token_counter: TokenCounter | None = None` argument on `ContextEditingMiddleware.__init__` that, when provided, is used to evaluate edit triggers - mirroring the `token_counter` parameter that `SummarizationMiddleware` already exposes.

### Use Case

`count_tokens_approximately` assumes ~4 chars/token, which fits English prose but systematically under-counts CJK-heavy conversations by 2-3x (measured 1.4-2.1 chars/token against provider-reported `usage_metadata` on Chinese financial filings and HTML tables with Qwen models). With the estimate reading 2-3x low, `ClearToolUsesEdit.trigger` fires far later than configured, which silently defeats threshold-based context management for CJK workloads.

The `"model"` counting mode is not a general fallback: many OpenAI-compatible providers/gateways do not implement `get_num_tokens_from_messages`.

### Proposed Solution
```python
from functools import partial
from langchain_core.messages.utils import count_tokens_approximately

middleware = ContextEditingMiddleware(
    edits=[ClearToolUsesEdit(trigger=120_000, keep=12)],
    token_counter=partial(count_tokens_approximately, chars_per_token=2.0),
)
```

- `token_counter` takes precedence over `token_count_method` when provided (same precedence model as `SummarizationMiddleware`).
- The module already defines the public `TokenCounter` type alias, and `ContextEdit.apply()` already receives a `count_tokens` argument - the extension point exists everywhere except the middleware's public API.
- Fully backwards compatible; no new dependencies.

### Alternatives Considered

1. Subclassing the middleware and overriding `wrap_model_call` / `awrap_model_call` - works (it is what I do today), but requires duplicating both method bodies because the counter is a closure inside them.
2. `token_count_method="model"` - unavailable on many OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
3. Tuning `ClearToolUsesEdit.trigger` down by the miscount factor - brittle, since the actual chars-per-token ratio varies with content mix.

### Additional Context

An implementation with unit tests is ready in #39754 (opened before I was aware of the issue-first policy - apologies; happy to adjust the approach based on maintainer feedback).

### Social handles (optional)

### Feature Description

A web page document loader that uses DOM AST parsing to extract only structural content — headings, paragraphs, code blocks, and lists — while removing nav, scripts, ads, and footers before content reaches the LLM.

Current BeautifulSoup-based loaders pass large amounts of markup-derived noise into context. This loader would strip that noise at the DOM tree level before serialization, with an optional query-aware BM25 section filter that keeps only the most relevant sections.

from langchain_dompruner import DomPrunerLoader```
loader = DomPrunerLoader(
    url="https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio.html",
    query="create_task return value"  # optional — enables BM25 section filter
)
docs = loader.load()
```
No API key required. Runs via npx dompruner-mcp.

### Use Case

Building RAG pipelines that index web pages — documentation, articles, wikis. Current web loaders produce 10,000–50,000 tokens per page. With DOM AST extraction this drops to ~1,000 tokens on average across a variety of pages:

| Page | Current (est.) | DomPruner | Reduction |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Python asyncio docs | 21,783 tok | 1,328 tok | 93.9% |
| MDN Fetch API | 15,965 tok | 1,368 tok | 91.4% |
| Wikipedia | 56,754 tok | 679 tok | 98.8% |
| **Average (10 pages)** | **15,735 tok** | **1,019 tok** | **93.5%** |


A 93% token reduction per page significantly lowers indexing cost and allows more documents within the same context budget. For multi-page RAG workflows the savings compound.

### Proposed Solution

Implement as a DomPrunerLoader following the standard BaseLoader interface. I've already built the underlying extraction engine as an open-source MCP server and benchmarked it against real web fetches. Happy to implement the LangChain adapter and submit a PR once maintainers confirm the right home for this (standalone langchain-dompruner package vs. another location given langchain-community deprecation).

### Alternatives Considered

- WebBaseLoader (BeautifulSoup): passes full markup, averaging ~15k tokens per page
- UnstructuredHTMLLoader: better for unstructured content, weaker on structured docs and API references
- PlaywrightURLLoader: handles JS-rendered content but still passes full HTML to the LLM
- FireCrawlLoader: external paid API dependency
- Manual post-processing of loader output: fragile, page-specific, no semantic ranking

### Additional Context

The extraction engine is open-source (MIT): https://github.com/dong7812/dompruner-mcp

Benchmark methodology: token counts measured against Anthropic's web_fetch_20260209 server tool (input_tokens from API response = actual tokens entering Claude's context), not estimated from raw HTML size.

title: Pattern: mechanical process verification for agent tool execution
body:
# Pattern: mechanical process verification for agent tool execution

## The observation

I've been measuring AI coding reliability for 2 months — not just code correctness, but whether the agent actually does what it says it did. The finding that surprised me:

| What the check examines | Triggers | False positives |
|-------------------------|----------|:--------------:|
| Filesystem facts (timestamps, paths) | 4–24 | 0% |
| Command strings (what was actually run) | 6 | 0% |
| Text-based ("did human confirm?") | 295 | 100% |

The first two work because the model *cannot fabricate filesystem metadata or command history*. The third fails because anything the model can generate as text, it can fake. 295 trigger events, zero real violations — the AI had written a 2-line script to auto-answer "yes."

The architectural property: mechanical checks and semantic review have **non-overlapping blind spots**. Mechanical checks miss stale rules and intent drift. Semantic review misses uniform-rater collapse (κ→0). Combined, their joint false-negative rate approaches zero — defense-in-depth applied to agent verification.

**Important context on the data**: these experiments ran on Claude Code's PreToolUse hooks (which can block tool calls via `exit 2`), not on LangChain. I'm sharing the *pattern*, not claiming direct evidence for LangChain's execution model.

## Why I'm sharing this here

LangChain's middleware API (`wrap_tool_call`, `before_model`) is the strategic direction for customizing agent behavior. The prebuilt middleware suite (PIIMiddleware, ToolCallLimitMiddleware, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware, etc.) covers content safety, cost control, and resilience.

But there's a category I haven't seen covered: **process integrity** — verifying that the action an agent claims to have taken actually happened in the environment. Content safety asks "is the output safe?" Process integrity asks "did the operation actually execute?"

I don't know if this category matters to LangChain users. The data I have is from AI coding (terminal/IDE agents), not from the customer-support/data-pipeline/automation deployments that LangChain serves. The pattern might not transfer. Or it might, in a different shape.

## Where I think it might fit

My tentative read: this lands in the **middleware API**, not callbacks and not LangGraph interrupts. Here's a rough sketch of why — not a proposal, just something concrete to react to:
```python
# Hypothetical: a middleware that cross-checks tool results
# against a light verifier function.
class ProcessGateMiddleware(BaseToolCallMiddleware):
    def __init__(self, verifiers: dict[str, Callable]):
        self.verifiers = verifiers  # tool_name → verifier_fn

    def after_tool_call(self, tool_call, result):
        verifier = self.verifiers.get(tool_call["name"])
        if verifier and not verifier(tool_call, result):
            return ToolMessage(
                content="Process gate failed: action was not verified",
                tool_call_id=tool_call["id"],
                status="error",
            )
        return result
```

A `file_write` tool might verify that a corresponding `file_read` happened within 30 seconds. A `db_query` tool might verify the result against a known-good query plan. The verifier functions are user-supplied; the middleware provides the hook and the audit trail.

This might be completely wrong. The API shape might need `wrap_tool_call` instead, or it might belong in LangGraph's state machine. Happy to be corrected — giving a concrete sketch beats asking an abstract question.

## What I'm proposing

A discussion about whether process-integrity verification fills a gap in LangChain's middleware ecosystem, and if so, what shape an integration should take.

## What I'm doing regardless

Building a standalone package that implements process-integrity gates (filesystem timestamps, command-string allowlisting — the two types with the strongest data behind them). If it works for LangChain users, great. If it never finds a fit, I'll write up what I learned. Either way, the data earns its keep.

---

*Context: undergrad, 2-month AI coding reliability experiment, 339 audit logs, 38 mechanical gates. Learning where the pattern fits (or doesn't) in the broader agent ecosystem. Here to listen, not to pitch.*

### Related Issues / PRs

_No response_

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
import asyncio
from langchain_core.callbacks import AsyncCallbackManager, AsyncCallbackHandler

received = []

class H(AsyncCallbackHandler):
    def __init__(self, name, run_inline):
        self.name = name
        self.run_inline = run_inline
    async def on_llm_start(self, *args, **kwargs):
        received.append(self.name)

mgr = AsyncCallbackManager(handlers=[H("inline", True), H("non_inline", False)])
asyncio.run(mgr.on_llm_start({}, ["hi"]))
print(received)  # got: ['inline']   expected: ['inline', 'non_inline']
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell

```

### Description

`AsyncCallbackManager.on_llm_start` dispatches to non-inline handlers only when there are zero inline handlers.

Location: `libs/core/langchain_core/callbacks/manager.py` (the `if inline_handlers: ... else: non_inline_tasks...` block in `on_llm_start`). Because the `else` runs only when no inline handler exists, registering any inline handler suppresses `on_llm_start` for every non-inline handler.

Real-world trigger: `LangChainTracer` (the LangSmith tracer) sets `run_inline = True`. So in any async app with tracing enabled, a custom `AsyncCallbackHandler` (non-inline by default) never receives `on_llm_start` for completion-style LLMs, yet still receives `on_llm_end` (dispatched to all handlers). Handlers that track state per run get an end with no start.

The sibling `on_chat_model_start` is correct: it loops over `self.handlers`, builds a per-handler task, and classifies each by `handler.run_inline`. `on_llm_start` should mirror that.

Disclosure: this was found and fixed with AI assistance. I have a branch with the fix (mirroring `on_chat_model_start`) plus a regression test that fails before and passes after, and would like to be assigned before opening the PR.

langchain-core current master / latest. Python 3.13.

body:
### Submission checklist

- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangChain rather than my code.
- [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangChain (or the specific integration package).
- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Package (Required)

- [x] langchain-openai

### Related Issues / PRs

#25510 reported the same missing-refusal behaviour in 2024 and was closed as stale by the
triage bot in March 2025, not by a maintainer decision — four people commented on it over
the following year saying they still hit it (the last in October 2025).

#34616 then made the non-streaming path raise `OpenAIRefusalError`. That is what makes
this worth reopening as a distinct problem: the two paths now disagree, which was not the
case when #25510 was filed.

The Responses API path already records refusals — see
`test__construct_lc_result_from_responses_api_refusal_response`, which asserts
`additional_kwargs["refusal"]`. Only Chat Completions streaming is missing it.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

Runs as-is, no API key or network required — it drives the same converters the streaming
and non-streaming paths use.
```python
from functools import reduce

from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, AIMessageChunk
from langchain_openai.chat_models.base import (
    OpenAIRefusalError,
    _convert_delta_to_message_chunk,
    _oai_structured_outputs_parser,
)
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Answer(BaseModel):
    """An answer."""

    text: str


REFUSAL = "I'm sorry, I cannot comply with that request."

# Non-streaming: `_create_chat_result` records the refusal on the message.
non_streamed = AIMessage(content="", additional_kwargs={"refusal": REFUSAL})
try:
    _oai_structured_outputs_parser(non_streamed, Answer)
except Exception as exc:
    print("non-streaming ->", type(exc).__name__, exc)

# Streaming: OpenAI sends the refusal on `delta.refusal`
# (`openai.types.chat.chat_completion_chunk.ChoiceDelta` declares the field).
deltas = [
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "", "refusal": "I'm sorry, "},
    {"refusal": "I cannot comply with that request."},
]
chunks = [_convert_delta_to_message_chunk(d, AIMessageChunk) for d in deltas]
streamed = reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, chunks)
print("streamed additional_kwargs ->", streamed.additional_kwargs)
try:
    _oai_structured_outputs_parser(
        AIMessage(content=streamed.content, additional_kwargs=streamed.additional_kwargs),
        Answer,
    )
except Exception as exc:
    print("streaming ->", type(exc).__name__, str(exc).splitlines()[0])
```

Output:
```text
non-streaming -> OpenAIRefusalError I'm sorry, I cannot comply with that request.
streamed additional_kwargs -> {}
streaming -> ValueError Structured Output response does not have a 'parsed' field nor a 'refusal' field. Received message:
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```text
ValueError: Structured Output response does not have a 'parsed' field nor a 'refusal' field. Received message:

content='' additional_kwargs={} response_metadata={} tool_calls=[] invalid_tool_calls=[]
```

### Description

When a model refuses a structured-output request, the wording it gives back is lost while
streaming, and the caller gets an error that describes langchain's internal state instead
of the refusal.

`openai.types.chat.chat_completion_chunk.ChoiceDelta` declares a `refusal` field, so
OpenAI streams refusals the same way it streams content. But
`_convert_delta_to_message_chunk` never reads it, and neither does
`_convert_chunk_to_generation_chunk`, so the aggregated chunk carries
`additional_kwargs == {}`.

The non-streaming path does record it, in `_create_chat_result`:
```python
if hasattr(message, "refusal"):
    generations[0].message.additional_kwargs["refusal"] = message.refusal
```

`_oai_structured_outputs_parser` then checks `parsed`, `additional_kwargs["refusal"]`, a
`non_standard` refusal content block, and `tool_calls` in turn. A streamed refusal misses
all four and falls through to the generic `ValueError`, so:

* non-streaming raises `OpenAIRefusalError` carrying the model's explanation;
* streaming raises a `ValueError` about a missing field, and the explanation is gone.

There is a second, narrower gap in the same area: `_create_chat_result` only reads
`refusal` when the response `isinstance(response, openai.BaseModel)`. An
OpenAI-compatible endpoint used through `ChatOpenAI(base_url=...)` that returns plain
dicts therefore loses the refusal in the non-streaming path too, because
`_convert_dict_to_message` does not read the field either.

Expected behaviour: a refusal should reach `additional_kwargs["refusal"]` regardless of
whether the response was streamed, so `OpenAIRefusalError` is raised consistently with the
model's wording. Recording it in the delta converter is enough for the streaming case —
chunk merging already concatenates same-key strings, which reassembles a refusal split
across deltas.

Python: 3.12.11
Platform: macOS-15.5-arm64
```

title: Prompt templates silently misrender or reject non-`dict` `Mapping` inputs (`ChainMap`, `MappingProxyType`, `UserDict`)
body:
### Submission checklist

- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.
- [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangChain rather than my code.
- [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangChain (or the specific integration package).
- [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package.
- [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS.

### Package (Required)

- [x] langchain-core

### Related Issues / PRs

Related to #39678 / #39680, which changed the same `dict` check to `Mapping` inside
`langchain_core/utils/mustache.py`. That fix covers nested *values* inside mustache
templates; the top-level `invoke` input is validated elsewhere and still only accepts
`dict`, so the problem remains for every template format.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)
```python
from collections import ChainMap, UserDict
from types import MappingProxyType

from langchain_core.prompts import PromptTemplate

single = PromptTemplate.from_template("Hello {name}")
multi = PromptTemplate.from_template("{greeting} {name}")

for cls in (dict, ChainMap, UserDict, MappingProxyType):
    print(cls.__name__, "->", single.invoke(cls({"name": "Alice"})).to_string())

for cls in (dict, ChainMap, UserDict, MappingProxyType):
    try:
        print(cls.__name__, "->", multi.invoke(cls({"greeting": "Hello", "name": "Alice"})).to_string())
    except TypeError as exc:
        print(cls.__name__, "-> TypeError:", exc)
```

Output:
```text
dict -> Hello Alice
ChainMap -> Hello ChainMap({'name': 'Alice'})
UserDict -> Hello {'name': 'Alice'}
mappingproxy -> Hello {'name': 'Alice'}

dict -> Hello Alice
ChainMap -> TypeError: Expected mapping type as input to PromptTemplate. Received <class 'collections.ChainMap'>.
UserDict -> TypeError: Expected mapping type as input to PromptTemplate. Received <class 'collections.UserDict'>.
mappingproxy -> TypeError: Expected mapping type as input to PromptTemplate. Received <class 'mappingproxy'>.
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```text
TypeError: Expected mapping type as input to PromptTemplate. Received <class 'collections.ChainMap'>.
For troubleshooting, visit: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/errors/INVALID_PROMPT_INPUT
```

### Description

`BasePromptTemplate._validate_input` decides how to interpret the value passed to
`invoke` / `ainvoke` using `isinstance(inner_input, dict)`. Standard-library mappings
that are not `dict` subclasses therefore take the wrong branch:

* **Single-variable templates** fall into the "bare value" convenience path, so the
  mapping is bound to the sole variable and rendered via `str()`. The result is a
  prompt containing the mapping's repr instead of the intended substitution, with no
  warning — the failure is silent, which is the more damaging case because it reaches
  the model.
* **Multi-variable templates** raise `TypeError` stating that a mapping type was
  expected, even though the input *is* a `Mapping`. The message contradicts the check
  that produced it.

`dict` subclasses (`OrderedDict`, `defaultdict`) are unaffected, so the boundary is
exactly "is it a `dict` subclass", not "is it a mapping":

| input type | `dict` subclass | single-variable template | multi-variable template |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `dict` | yes | `Hello Alice` | ok |
| `OrderedDict` | yes | `Hello Alice` | ok |
| `defaultdict` | yes | `Hello Alice` | ok |
| `ChainMap` | no | `Hello ChainMap({'name': 'Alice'})` | `TypeError` |
| `UserDict` | no | `Hello {'name': 'Alice'}` | `TypeError` |
| `MappingProxyType` | no | `Hello {'name': 'Alice'}` | `TypeError` |

These are not exotic types: `ChainMap` is a natural fit for layered defaults, and
`MappingProxyType` is what you get from `vars(obj)` or any read-only config surface.
All template formats are affected, since every one of them goes through
`_validate_input`, and both the sync and async paths share it.

Expected behaviour: any `Mapping` should be accepted as the variable mapping, matching
both the error message's own wording and the resolution of #39678.

The fix looks like a one-line change (`isinstance(inner_input, Mapping)`, converting to
`dict` for the declared return type). Happy to open a PR with regression tests if this
looks right.

import runpy

from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from unittest.mock import Mock, patch

from langchain_model_profiles.cli import refresh

payload = {
    "anthropic": {
        "id": "anthropic",
        "name": "Anthropic",
        "models": {
            "null-model": {
                "id": "null-model",
                "name": "true false null",
                "tool_call": True,
                "limit": {"context": 200000, "output": 4096},
                "modalities": {"input": ["text"], "output": ["text"]},
            }
        },
    }
}

response = Mock()
response.json.return_value = payload
response.raise_for_status = Mock()

with TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    data_dir = Path(tmp)
    with (
        patch("langchain_model_profiles.cli.httpx.get", return_value=response),
        patch("builtins.input", return_value="y"),
    ):
        refresh("anthropic", data_dir)

    profiles = runpy.run_path(str(data_dir / "_profiles.py"))["_PROFILES"]
    print({model_id: profile["name"] for model_id, profile in profiles.items()})

    assert "null-model" in profiles
    assert profiles["null-model"]["name"] == "true false null"
    assert profiles["null-model"]["tool_calling"] is True
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)
```shell
{'None-model': 'True False None'}
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
AssertionError

The generated Python remains syntactically valid, so this is silent data corruption rather than a generation error.
```

### Description

`langchain-profiles refresh` serializes the merged profile dictionary with `json.dumps`, then converts JSON literals to Python literals with three global string replacements:
```python
json_str.replace("true", "True").replace("false", "False").replace("null", "None")
```

Those replacements also run inside quoted JSON keys and values. A model ID such as `null-model` becomes `None-model`, and an ordinary profile string such as `true false null` becomes `True False None`. Because both results are still valid Python strings, the generated module imports successfully with altered data.

I expect only unquoted JSON literal tokens to become Python `True`, `False`, and `None`; every key and string value should round-trip exactly. I verified that a token-aware conversion using the standard-library `tokenize` module preserves the current generated formatting for normal payloads, preserves quoted strings, and still converts actual booleans/nulls. A focused regression test can generate and import `_profiles.py` to cover both behaviors.

The current models.dev payload does not appear to contain a lowercase `true`, `false`, or `null` substring in its model IDs or names, so I have not found an already-corrupted shipped entry. The bug is nevertheless deterministic for valid future provider data or augmentation strings.

If this approach is aligned, please assign the issue to @uczltw6 and I will submit the tested patch. The reproduction, investigation, and proposed implementation were prepared with Codex assistance.

### Description

On Windows, two langchain-core unit tests fail on current master.

`test_from_file_encoding` attempts to reopen a `NamedTemporaryFile` while the file is still open. Windows keeps the file locked and raises `PermissionError`.

The proposed fix uses `sys.executable` for isolated imports and pytest's `tmp_path` fixture for the encoding test. This preserves the existing assertions while making both tests deterministic across platforms.

After applying the fix, the complete langchain-core unit suite passes: 2218 passed, 3 skipped, 9 xfailed, and 2 xpassed.
